content.text:
What kind of story is Daddy-Long-Legs?

Daddy-Long-Legs is a warm coming-of-age tale about Judy, an orphanage girl who grows her dreams by writing letters to a benefactor she has never even seen. It carries the message that someone's care and belief can make a child's dream bloom.

The original story of Daddy-Long-Legs

This is an epistolary coming-of-age novel published in 1912 by the American author Jean Webster. Judy, who grew up in an orphanage, gets to attend school thanks to an anonymous benefactor, and she grows up writing letters to him. The heartwarming twist is that the benefactor turns out to be a kind man who had been close to her all along.

content.text:
A summary of the Daddy-Long-Legs plot

Judy, who loved books and writing, gets to attend school thanks to an anonymous benefactor who noticed her writing talent. Because of the long shadow she once saw beyond the fence, she calls him "Daddy-Long-Legs" and writes him letters. When she meets a kind gentleman during vacation and learns he was Daddy-Long-Legs all along, the two come to live like family.
content.caption: A warm twist

content.text:
The lessons of Daddy-Long-Legs

The heart of it is that someone's warm care and belief nurtures dreams, and a grateful heart for the help you receive is precious. Try talking with your child about, "Who is someone who cheers on your dreams?"
content.caption: A grateful heart

content.alt: Daddy-Long-Legs - How to read it to your child
content.text:
How to read it to your child

Read the scenes of Judy writing her letters in a warm tone, and at the twist ("Huh? It's you, sir!") pause for a moment and enjoy the surprise together. Lead into gratitude with, "If you wrote a letter to someone you're thankful for, what would you say?" Suitable for ages 5-7.
content.caption: Reading that shares gratitude

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What age is Daddy-Long-Legs good for?
A. It's suitable for ages 5-7. With themes of dreams and gratitude, it's great for the age when children begin to take an interest in peer relationships and their own dreams.

Q. Won't the letter format be too difficult?
A. The picture-book version for young children focuses on the warmth of the letters and the growing-up story, so it comes across gently.

Q. What activities pair well with it?
A. Writing a letter to someone you're thankful for, thinking of "people who cheer me on," and drawing your dreams all work well.
